To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the diffusion of moisture into both tetragional and cubic single crystal zirconias was the same, irrespective whether the crystals were immersed in water or exposed to moisture gas, and that the oxygen diffusivity in zirconia was consistent with that reported for higher temperatures.

oxygen diffuses in both tetragolar and cubic zirconia at temperatures characteristic of the low-temperature degradation (LTD) of tetragonal ZrO2, and that the diffusion of hydrogen and deuterium in tetragonal ZO2 is consistent with the diffusion of oxygen.

the oxygen diffusivity in tetragonal and in cubic single crystals is the same irrespective of whether the crystal is exposed to a water vapor or gas environment, and that the diffusivity of oxygen is consistent with the reported activation energy of 0.9 eV for oxygen diffusion in the cubic crystal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the diffusion of moisture-related ions and molecules in zirconia.
the diffusion of H, D and O18 species into single crystal zirconias at temperatures of 100° to 220°C.
the diffusion of water-related species into zirconia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the diffusion of H and D into tetragonal single crystals is possible but the diffusion of moisture-related ions is not.
oxygen vacancies are the only species that diffuse in zirconium dioxide.
the diffusion of moisture-related ions in yttria-stabilized zirconia is not the mechanism for moisture-enhanced low temperature degradation of tetragonally stabilized zirconia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diffusion of water species into zirconia is negligible at room temperature, and that the diffusion of H or OH is not the cause of the low-temperature degradation.
oxygen vacancies in zirconia are mobile at temperatures as low as 100°C and can be filled by oxygen from either a gas or water environment.
the oxygen diffusivity in tetragonal and the cubic crystal is identical, that H and D can diffuse in the tetragional zirconia, but that neither H nor D can diffuse in cubic zirconia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diffusion of water species into zirconia at low temperatures is not the mechanism for low-temperature degradation.

moisture does not enhance the low-temperature degradation process by diffusing in zirconia and reacting with oxygen vacancies to form hydroxyls, which are the precursors to the formation of the metastable tetragonal phase.

oxygen diffuses in zirconia much more easily than moisture-related species, even at temperatures as low as 100°C, and therefore moisture-enhanced low temperature degradation of zirconia is due to a mechanism that does not involve diffusion of moisture-related ions.
